title: Epistolary Jurisdiction — Converting Letters & Postcards into Writs

content.overview: Epistolary jurisdiction allows a court to treat a letter or informal communication as a writ petition where the writer lacks means or access to counsel and alleges serious public or fundamental-rights wrongs, subject to screening for genuineness. It is access practice within Articles 32 and 226, not a new writ.
content.glance: Ask: (1) Letter treated as petition after screening? (2) Access barrier? (3) Serious public/FR wrong? (4) Forum 32 or 226? (5) Genuineness checked?
content.study:
Core rule: Formal pleadings can shut out the poor and remote. Epistolary practice converts genuine informal communications into proceedings under Articles 32 or 226 after screening.

Aligned with companion thin topic epistolary-jurisdiction. Not a licence for anonymous or motivated campaigns. Abuse filters apply.

Case-law verification remains separate.

sections.heading: Meaning
sections.body: Letter or informal writing treated as initiating process after screening for genuineness and justiciability.

sections.heading: Access purpose
sections.body: Aids persons without means or counsel who allege serious public or fundamental-rights wrongs.

sections.heading: Screening
sections.body: Identity, factual basis, and bona fides checked; anonymous/motivated campaigns may be rejected.

sections.heading: Forum
sections.body: Still Article 32 or 226; epistolary practice does not enlarge subject-matter jurisdiction.

sections.heading: After registration
sections.body: Ordinary writ process and abuse filters apply.

examples.title: Remote complainant letter
examples.body: Letter alleging denial of statutory entitlements to a remote class; court may screen and register under 226.

examples.title: Anonymous campaign
examples.body: Unsigned political attack letter — screening allows rejection.

hypotheticals.question: Must every letter be registered as PIL?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Conversion is discretionary and screened.
